## SVD and Diagonalization
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
SVD is another factorization techinique that uses the concepts of eigenvalues and eigenvectors. It is similar to diagonalization, but does not create $PDP^{-1}$.

The eigenvectors in $P$ have three big problems: 

1. They are usually not orthogonal.
2. There are not always enough eigenvectors.
3. They can only be found for square matrices. 

SVD solves  all those problems.

SVD applies to _any_ matrix, no matter its size, symmetry, invertibility, or diagonalizability.
:::

## SVD in Data Science

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
Consider a dataset where rows represent users and columns represent movies. Each entry in the matrix indicates the rating a user has given to a movie. 

$${\mbox{$m$ data objects}}\left\{\begin{array}{c}\;\\\;\\\;\\\;\\\;\end{array}\right.\;\;\overbrace{\left[\begin{array}{ccccc}
\begin{array}{c}a_{11}\\\vdots\\a_{i1}\\\vdots\\a_{m1}\end{array}&
\begin{array}{c}\dots\\\ddots\\\dots\\\ddots\\\dots\end{array}&
\begin{array}{c}a_{1j}\\\vdots\\a_{ij}\\\vdots\\a_{mj}\end{array}&
\begin{array}{c}\dots\\\ddots\\\dots\\\ddots\\\dots\end{array}&
\begin{array}{c}a_{1n}\\\vdots\\a_{in}\\\vdots\\a_{mn}\end{array}
\end{array}\right]}^{\mbox{$n$ features}}$$

SVD "compresses" such a matrix of real-world messy data into matrices of smaller dimensions.
:::

## SVD in Data Science

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
SVD produces three matrices: <br>

$m \times r$ matrix $U$, $r \times r$ matrix $\Sigma,$ and $r \times n$ matrix $V^\top$. 

::: {.center-text}
![](/images/01-svd.png){style="position: absolute; right: 12rem; width: 60%; height: 60%;"}
:::
:::

## SVD in Data Science

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
$$\begin{align*}
A &= (U \Sigma) V^{\top} \\
\mbox{$m$}\left\{\begin{array}{c}\;\\\;\\\;\\\;\\\;\end{array}\right.\;\;\underbrace{\left[\begin{array}{cccc}\begin{array}{c}\vdots\\\vdots\\{\bf a_1}\\\vdots\\\vdots\end{array}&\begin{array}{c}\vdots\\\vdots\\{\bf a_2}\\\vdots\\\vdots\end{array}&\dots&\begin{array}{c}\vdots\\\vdots\\{\bf a_n}\\\vdots\\\vdots\end{array}\\\end{array}\right]}_{\mbox{$n$}} &=
\underbrace{\left[\begin{array}{cc}\vdots&\vdots\\\vdots&\vdots\\\sigma_1\mathbf{u}_1&\sigma_r\mathbf{u}_r\\\vdots&\vdots\\\vdots&\vdots\end{array}\right]}_{\large r}
\times
\left[\begin{array}{ccccc}\dots&\dots&\mathbf{v}_1&\dots&\dots\\\dots&\dots&\mathbf{v}_r&\dots&\dots\end{array}\right]
\end{align*}$$
$U\Sigma$ contains a row for each user, while $V^\top$ contains a column for each movie. 

The columns of $U\Sigma$ and rows of $V^\top$ can correspond to various movie characteristics, such as genre, target audience, production quality, etc.

<!-- We have transformed objects from an $n$-dimensional space to a 
$r$-dimensional space, where $r$ is (probably much) smaller than $n$. -->
:::

<!-- ## Geometric View

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
SVD applies to _any_ matrix, no matter its size, (a)symmetry, invertibility, or diagonalizability.

<br>

Geometrically, an $m \times n$ matrix represents a linear transformation that maps vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$ to vectors in $\mathbb{R}^m$. 

SVD decomposes an $m \times n$ matrix into a sequence of three steps.

1. Rotation within $\mathbb{R}^n$, without scaling.

2. Scaling each dimension $i$ by a constant $\sigma_i$, called a __singular value__.

3. Rotation within $\mathbb{R}^m$. Note that this is _not_ necessarily the inverse of step 1. The rotation might be by a different angle, across a different axis, and in a space of different dimension.

:::

## Geometric View

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
::: {.center-text}
![](/images/18-svd-geometric.png){style="position: absolute; right: 12rem; width: 60%; height: 80%;"}
:::

::: -->

## Symmetric Matrices
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
Given an $m \times n$ matrix $A$, the $n \times n$ matrix $A^\top A$ is always symmetric because

$$
(A^\top A)^\top = A^\top (A^\top)^\top = (A^\top A).
$$

Hence, $A^\top A$ can be _**orthogonally diagonalized**_. 

This implies that 

- $A^\top A$ has $n$ linearly independent eigenvectors

- these eigenvectors can form an orthonormal set
:::


## Singular Values

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}

Let $\{\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_n\}$ be a set consisting of orthonormal eigenvectors of $A^\top A$. 

Let $\lambda_1, \dots, \lambda_n$ be the corresponding eigenvalues of $A^\top A$.  

Then, for any eigenvector $\mathbf{v}_i$, 

$$\begin{align*}
\Vert A\mathbf{v}_i\Vert^2 &= (A\mathbf{v}_i)^\top A\mathbf{v}_i \\
&= \mathbf{v}_i^\top A^\top A\mathbf{v}_i \\
&= \mathbf{v}_i^\top (\lambda_i\mathbf{v}_i) \; \hphantom{\lambda_i} \text{(since $\mathbf{v}_i$ is an eigenvector of $A^{\top} A$)} \\
&= \lambda_i (\mathbf{v}_i^\top \mathbf{v}_i) \; \hphantom{\lambda_i}  \\
&= \lambda_i \; \hphantom{\mathbf{v}_i^\top (\lambda_i)\mathbf{v}_i} \text{(since $\mathbf{v}_i$ is a unit vector).}
\end{align*}$$

Since $\Vert\cdot\Vert^2$ is nonnegative, the eigenvalues of $A^\top A$ are all nonnegative.
:::

## Singular Values

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}

Since all eigenvalues of $A^\top A$ are nonnegative, their square roots are going to be real numbers.


```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <p><span class="label">Singular values</span>
        The <b>singular values</b> of \(A\) are the square roots of the eigenvalues of \(A^\top A\).  
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```
They are denoted by $\sigma_1,\dots,\sigma_n,$ and by convention they are arranged in decreasing order.


That is, $\sigma_i = \sqrt{\lambda_i}$ for $i = 1,\dots,n$ where $\lambda_i$ denotes an eigenvalue of $A^\top A$ and we can reorder the singular values so that

$$\sigma_1 \geq \sigma_2 \geq \cdots \geq \sigma_n \geq 0.$$

<!-- Note that by the argument on the previous slide _the singular values of $A$ are the lengths of the vectors $A\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, A\mathbf{v}_n.$_ -->
:::

## Singular Values
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
__Example.__ Consider 
$$A = \begin{bmatrix}
    4 & 0\\
    3 & -5
\end{bmatrix}.$$
Let us find the singular values of $A$. 

First, we compute $A^TA$:

$$A^TA =  \begin{bmatrix}
    4 & 3\\ 0 & -5
\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix}
    4 & 0 \\ 3 & -5
\end{bmatrix} = 
\begin{bmatrix}
    25 & -15 \\
    -15 & 25
\end{bmatrix}.$$

Note that the resulting matrix is symmetric!
:::

## Singular Values
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
To find the eigenvalues of $A^TA$ we need to compute its characteristic polynomial.
$$\det(A^TA - \lambda I) = \det\left( \begin{bmatrix}
    25 - \lambda & -15\\
    -15 & 25 - \lambda
\end{bmatrix} \right) $$
$$= \lambda^2 - 50 \lambda+400 = (\lambda-10)(\lambda-40).$$
Hence, the eigenvalues of $A^\top A$ are $\lambda_1 = 40$ and $\lambda_2 = 10$. 

The corresponding singular values are $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{40}$ and $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{10}.$<br>
:::

## Singular Vectors
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}

<!-- We know that vectors $\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_n$ form an orthogonal set because they are eigenvectors of the symmetric matrix $A^\top A$.   -->

```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <p><span class="label">Right singular vectors</span>
        The eigenvectors \(\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, \mathbf{v}_n\) of \(A^\top A,\) that form an orthonormal set, are known as the <b>right singular vectors</b> of \(A.\)
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```

It can be shown that $A\mathbf{v}_1, \dots, A\mathbf{v}_n$ form an orthogonal set as well. <br>
Since $\Vert A\mathbf{v}_i\Vert^2 = \lambda_i = \sigma_i^2,$ the length of $A{\bf v}_i$ is equal to $\sigma_i.$

If we define the vectors ${\bf u}_i$ such that $A{\bf v}_i = \sigma_i{\bf u}_i$, then ${\bf u}_i$ must be a unit vector. 

```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <p><span class="label">Left singular vectors</span>
        The vectors \({\bf u}_1, {\bf u}_2, \ldots, {\bf u}_m\) with \(\mathbf{u}_i =  \frac{1}{\sigma_i}A\mathbf{v}_i\) are called the <b>left singular vectors</b> of \(A.\) 
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```

:::

## Singular Value Decomposition
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
```{python}
from IPython.core.display import HTML

def generate_html():
    return r"""
    <div class="purple-box">
        <p><span class="label">Singular Value Decomposition</span>
        Let \(A\) be an \(m\times n\) matrix with rank \(r\).  Then there exist 
        <ul> <li> an \(r\times r\) matrix \(\Sigma\) whose diagonal entries are the first \(r\) singular values of \(A\), \(\sigma_1 \geq \sigma_2 \geq \dots \geq \sigma_r > 0,\)
            <li> an \(m\times r\) orthonormal matrix \(U\) whose columns are left singular vectors of \(A\),
            <li> an \(n\times r\) orthonormal matrix \(V\) whose columns are right singular vectors of \(A\),
        </li>
        <br>
        such that 
        \(A = U\Sigma V^{\top}.\)
        </p>
    </div>
    """
html_content = generate_html()
display(HTML(html_content))
```
__Proof.__ See notes.
:::


## Singular Value Decomposition
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
__Example.__ Let us return to
$$A = \begin{bmatrix}
    4 & 0\\
    3 & -5
\end{bmatrix}$$
and find its singular value decomposition.

Since its singular values are $\sigma_1 = \sqrt{40}$ and $\sigma_2 = \sqrt{10},$ we find $$\Sigma = \begin{bmatrix}
    \sqrt{40} & 0\\
    0 & \sqrt{10}
\end{bmatrix}.$$

Next, we need to find the right and left singular vectors of $A$.
:::

## Singular Value Decomposition
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
<!-- Next, we find the right and left singular vectors of $A$. We will use them to construct orthonormal matrices $V$ and $U$ for the SVD of $A=U\Sigma V^\top.$  -->

The right singular vectors are defined as the normalized (and orthogonalized) eigenvectors of $A^TA.$

To find the eigenvectors of $A^TA$, we need to find the nullspace of $A^TA - \lambda_1I$ and $A^TA - \lambda_2I$.
$$A^TA - \lambda_1I = \begin{bmatrix}
    25 & -15 \\
    -15 & 25
\end{bmatrix} - 40 I = \begin{bmatrix} -15 & -15 \\ -15 & -15 \end{bmatrix} \sim 
\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 0\end{bmatrix}.$$
It follows that $x_2$ is free and $x_1 = -x_2.$ This implies that any vector of the form 
$s\begin{bmatrix}
    -1 \\ 1
\end{bmatrix}$, where $s$ is a scalar is an eigenvector corresponding to $\lambda_1$. 
:::

## Singular Value Decomposition
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
Since the SVD requires the eigenvector to have unit length, we take $\mathbf v_1 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix}$.<br>
Similarly, we find $\mathbf v_2 = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1\\ 1\end{bmatrix}$. <br>
From here it follows that 
$$V = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 & 1 \\ 1 & 1 \end{bmatrix}.$$

:::

## Singular Value Decomposition
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
It remains to find the left singular vectors
$$\mathbf u_1 = \frac{A \mathbf v_1}{\sigma_1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{40}} \begin{bmatrix}
    4 & 0 \\
    3 & 5 
\end{bmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}
    -1 \\ -2
\end{bmatrix}.$$
$$\mathbf u_2 = \frac{A \mathbf v_2}{\sigma_2} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{40}} \begin{bmatrix}
    4 & 0 \\
    3 & 5 
\end{bmatrix} \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\begin{bmatrix}
    2 \\ -1
\end{bmatrix}.$$
Hence, $U = \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \begin{bmatrix}
    -1 & 2 \\ -2 & -1
\end{bmatrix}.$

Together, $\Sigma, U,$ and $V$ form the singular value decomposition of $A$.
:::

## Singular Value Decomposition
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}

## Singular Value Decomposition
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
Let us find the SVD of the $3 \times 2$ matrix

$$A = \begin{bmatrix}4.6 & -2.8 \\ 6.8 & -7.4 \\ -4.4 & 9.2\end{bmatrix}.$$

Note that $\operatorname{rank}(A) = 2$.

<br> 

We are going to calculate the singular values, right singular vectors, and left singular vectors of $A$.
:::

## Step 1
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
To start, we compute the matrix

$$A^\top A =
\begin{bmatrix}4.6 & 6.8 & -4.4 \\ -2.8 & -7.4 & 9.2\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}4.6 & -2.8 \\ 6.8 & -7.4 \\ -4.4 & 9.2\end{bmatrix} = 
\begin{bmatrix} 86.76 & -103.68 \\ -103.68 & 147.24 \end{bmatrix}.
$$

Next, we must compute the eigenvalues of $A^\top A$ using the characteristic polynomial.

$$\begin{align*}
0 &= \det(A^\top A - \lambda I) \\
&= (86.76 - \lambda) (147.24 - \lambda) - (-103.68)^2 \\
&= \lambda^2 - 234 \lambda + 2025 \\
&= (\lambda - 225) (\lambda - 9).
\end{align*}$$
:::

## Step 1
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
The two eigenvalues of $A^\top A$ are 225 and 9 (by convention, we order the eigenvalues from largest to smallest). As a result, the singular values of $A$ are:

$$\sigma_1 = \sqrt{225} = 15 \text{ and } \sigma_2 = \sqrt{9} = 3.$$

Hence, the middle matrix in the SVD is:

$$\Sigma = \begin{bmatrix} 15 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}.$$

It is a diagonal matrix of the same shape as $A$, with the singular values on the main diagonal.
:::

## Step 2
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
Next, we must find the eigenvectors of $A^\top A$. To do so, we find the null spaces of

$$A^\top A - 225 I = \begin{bmatrix} -138.24 & -103.68 \\ -103.68 & -77.76 \end{bmatrix},$$
$$A^\top A - 9I = \begin{bmatrix} 77.76 & -103.68 \\ -103.68 & 138.24 \end{bmatrix}.$$

Both of these matrices have rank 1 because the second column is a scalar multiple of the first one. So both null spaces are 1-dimensional.

You can use Gauss-Jordan elimination to solve for the null spaces of the above matrices. 
:::

## Step 2
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
The resulting 1-dimensional null spaces are the span of the vectors

$$\mathbf{v}_1 = \begin{bmatrix} -3/5 \\ 4/5 \end{bmatrix}
\text{ and }
\mathbf{v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 4/5 \\ 3/5 \end{bmatrix},$$

respectively. These are the right singular vectors of A. Note that these vectors are orthogonal, and I have normalized them to be unit vectors.

Hence, the columns of the orthonormal matrix $V$ are ${\bf v}_1$ and ${\bf v}_2$. We then transpose it into:

$$V^\top = \begin{bmatrix} -3/5 & 4/5 \\ 4/5 & 3/5 \end{bmatrix}.$$
:::

## Step 3
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
We can calculate the first left singular vector ${\bf u}_1$ as follows.

$$\begin{align*}
{\bf u}_1 &= \frac{1}{\sigma_1} A {\bf v}_1 \\
& = \frac{1}{15} \begin{bmatrix}4.6 & -2.8 \\ 6.8 & -7.4 \\ -4.4 & 9.2\end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} -3/5 \\ 4/5 \end{bmatrix} \\
&= \begin{bmatrix} -1/3 \\ -2/3 \\ 2/3 \end{bmatrix} \\
\end{align*}$$

Note that ${\bf u}_1$ is a unit vector! That is, the length of $A {\bf v}_1$ is 15 -- the first singular value. After dividing by this singular value $\sigma_1$, the length is now 
1.
:::

## Step 3
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
We can use the same idea to calculate the second left singular vector.

$${\bf u}_2 = \frac{1}{\sigma_2} A {\bf v}_2 = \begin{bmatrix} 2/3 \\ 1/3 \\ 2/3 \end{bmatrix}.$$


We are so close now to the complete factorization! We have the first two columns of $U$, but not the final one yet.

$$A = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} -1/3 & 2/3 & \color{blue}{{\bf ?}} \\ -2/3 & 1/3 & \color{blue}{{\bf ?}} \\ 2/3 & 2/3 & \color{blue}{{\bf ?}} \end{bmatrix}}_{U} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 15 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}}_{\Sigma} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} -3/5 & 4/5 \\ 4/5 & 3/5 \end{bmatrix}}_{V^\top}.$$
:::

## Step 3
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
Here we have some good news and some bad news.

- The bad news: we cannot calculate the third column of $U$ as ${\bf u}_3 = \frac{1}{\sigma_3} A {\bf v}_3$ ... because there is no ${\bf v}_3$.

- The good news: in the matrix product $U \Sigma$, the entries in the third column are going to be multiplied by 0s.

Since we want $U$ to be an orthonormal matrix, the third column of $U$ must be a unit vector that is orthogonal to ${\bf u}_1$ and ${\bf u}_2$. We can find this using Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization! A possible answer is:

$${\bf u}_3 = \begin{bmatrix} -2/3 \\ 2/3 \\ 1/3 \end{bmatrix}.$$
:::

## Step 3
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
Putting everything together, the SVD of the matrix $A$ is:

$$A = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} -1/3 & 2/3 & -2/3 \\ -2/3 & 1/3 & 2/3 \\ 2/3 & 2/3 & 1/3 \end{bmatrix}}_{U} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 15 & 0 \\ 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 0 \end{bmatrix}}_{\Sigma} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} -3/5 & 4/5 \\ 4/5 & 3/5 \end{bmatrix}}_{V^\top}.$$

Note that calculating the SVD required many of the algebraic tools that we have learned over the course of this semester! We used Gauss-Jordan elimination, Gram-Schmidt orthogonalization, eigenvalues and eigenvectors, and more.
:::

## Singular Value Decomposition
:::{style="font-size: .8em"}

We can find the same result using Python.


```{python}

```

```{python}
#| echo: true
import numpy as np
A = np.array([[4.6, -2.8],
              [6.8, -7.4],
              [-4.4, 9.2]])
U, Sigma, V = np.linalg.svd(A)
print(U)
```

<!-- ## Key Ideas

:::{style="font-size: .8em"}
- The SVD factors $A$ into $U\Sigma V^\top.$
- $\Sigma$ is a diagonal matrix that contains the singular values of $A$. A singular value $\sigma_i$ is the square root of an eigenvalue of $A^\top A.$
- $U$ and $V$ are orthonormal matrices that contain left and right singular vectors of $A$, respectively. The right singular vectors are the normalized eigenvectors of $A^\top A.$ The left eigenvectors can be derived from the right eigenvectors.
::: -->
